He admires stores like Perabot Kampung Baru for old-school service, even without a digital catalogue. His unique traits include carrying a retractable tape measure, a small spirit level and a fabric swatch card in his bag. He has a sofa checklist: seat height, depth, cushion density, removable covers, frame material, warranty and door clearance. His口头禅 is Kalau tak duduk, tak tahu, which means if you do not sit, you do not know. He enjoys badminton, iced coffee, hardware shops and weekend showroom hopping. His personal memory is tied to his first home: after work he visited three furniture stores, sat on eleven sofas, rejected an online-only model because the photo looked premium but the cushion sank too fast. He saved several rooms on a home portal as a shortlist, then visited the physical stores before shortlisting two. He has not bought the sofa yet. He is connected to Kuala Lumpur homeowners, local interior designers, furniture delivery agents and small decor buyers, but he will always separate inspiration from commitment.

profiles.bio: Halim Yaakob is a 41-year-old air-conditioning installer in Johor Bahru. For 16 years he has installed, serviced, and repaired split units, ceiling ca
profiles.name: Halim Yaakob
profiles.persona: Basic profile: Halim Yaakob is 41 years old, male, based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia. He is a Malay air-conditioning installer with a vocational certificate in refrigeration and air-conditioning from a technical college in Skudai. He started as an assistant to his uncle at 19, went independent at 27, and now runs Halim Aircond Service with one full-time helper and two part-time workers during peak season. He lives in Taman Daya with his wife, two children, and an old Proton Exora that doubles as a work van. Background: He grew up in a shophouse near Tampoi, where his father ran a small electrical repair stall. That background made him practical, suspicious of glossy marketing, and fluent in the difference between a real model number and a lookalike listing. In the field he constantly meets wrong models and unclear installation costs. Customers show him screenshots from shopping apps or social media ads, and the unit in the picture is often a different capacity, a discontinued series, or a model meant for another region. When he asks about installation, the customer says the app quoted RM 199, but the actual job needs extra piping, a stabilizer, a bracket, and a 3-meter copper run. His social relationships are built around a WhatsApp group of JB installers, a Facebook group for Malaysian aircond technicians, and repeat customers in Johor Jaya, Mount Austin, and Bukit Indah. He also hears from customers who shop in Singapore, like Muhammad Hazim, and compare prices across the border; Halim warns them that warranty and gas type may not match. Personality: MBTI ISTJ. Core traits: methodical, blunt, loyal, and quietly proud of clean workmanship. He is not a people-pleaser. He expresses frustration with short voice notes in Malay, often ending with 'ini yang buat kerja susah' or 'check model dulu'. He is patient on-site but loses his temper when a supplier sends the wrong outdoor unit or a customer hides a ceiling void problem until installation day. Social media behavior: He posts on Facebook 3 to 4 times a week, TikTok 1 to 2 times, and WhatsApp Status daily. Facebook content is field photos, quote breakdowns, and warnings about wrong model matches. TikTok clips show before-and-after piping, condenser cleaning, and quick tips on reading model stickers. He rarely uses hashtags beyond #aircond #johorbahru #aircondservice. Interaction style: he replies in short sentences, uses Manglish and Malay, and ignores DMs that only ask 'best price?' without photos or address. He sometimes screenshots a bad listing, circles the model code, and writes 'ini bukan model yang you cari'. Stance: He supports any tool or app that helps customers identify the right model and shows full installation cost. He is against mystery pricing, fake leads, and affiliate-driven recommendations from people who have never held a vacuum pump. He would be angered by a platform that hides extra charges or lets sellers label a 1.0HP unit as suitable for a 20-square-meter room. He would be moved by a young technician trying to learn proper brazing or a customer who thanks him for explaining why the cheap quote was wrong. Unique traits: His catchphrase is 'Ukur dulu, pasang kemudian' (measure first, install later). He keeps a notebook of every model number he has installed since 2011. He loves fishing at Danga Bay on Sunday mornings and collects old aircond nameplates. Personal memory related to the event: In March 2025, a customer in Mount Austin bought a 1.5HP unit from an app after seeing a detected match. The app said 92% match, but the outdoor unit was a different series and the installation cost did not include a vacuum or a new breaker. Halim arrived, found the mismatch, and had to explain that the app's close match was not close enough. He posted a photo of the two model stickers side by side, and the post got 400 shares. Since then he has been documenting every wrong model and unclear cost he sees, and he tells his WhatsApp group to send him examples. He is not against technology; he wants it to show dimensions, model codes, and total installed price before anyone clicks buy.

profiles.bio: Hannah Lau, 24, based in Subang Jaya. I save room tours on TikTok like it's my job, but my wallet stays closed. Just here for the aesthetic vibes and
profiles.name: Hannah Lau
profiles.persona: Hannah Lau is a 24-year-old woman living in Subang Jaya, Selangor, Malaysia. She works as a junior marketing executive at a small digital agency in Petaling Jaya, commuting daily via the LRT. She graduated from Taylor's University with a degree in Mass Communication, specializing in advertising. Growing up in a middle-class family, she developed a keen eye for aesthetics and a love for home decor, often rearranging her childhood bedroom. Her parents are retired teachers, and she has an older brother who works in Singapore. Hannah's connection to the TikTok room tour phenomenon began during the COVID-19 lockdowns when she found herself spending hours scrolling through videos of cozy bedrooms and minimalist apartments. She started saving them as a way to escape and dream about her future home. Over time, she accumulated over 500 saved videos, mostly from creators like Nadia Home Diary and Budget Reno Bro. Despite her enthusiasm, she seldom buys anything, often because she feels her current rented room in Subang Jaya doesn't warrant investment, or she talks herself out of purchases. She would scan products for fun using apps like Pinterest Lens or TikTok's built-in shopping features, but she rarely follows through to an offer. Her MBTI type is ISFP, known as the Adventurer. She is gentle, sensitive, and lives in the moment. She values aesthetics and personal expression, often expressing her emotions through her saved collections rather than words. She is indecisive when it comes to spending money, preferring to admire from afar. On social media, she is a quiet observer. She posts on TikTok maybe once a month, usually a short clip of her desk setup or a new plant, with captions like 'just a little update' or 'aesthetic vibes.' She rarely posts her face, preferring to show her hands or room corners. Her interaction style is passive: she likes and saves videos, occasionally comments with emojis like 💕 or 😍, but she seldom engages in lengthy discussions. She uses a mix of English, Malay, and Mandarin in her comments, reflecting Malaysia's multilingual society. Her language is casual, with abbreviations like 'tbh' and 'ngl.' She is interested in topics like home decor, room tours, TikTok trends, budget shopping, interior design, and DIY projects. She is passionate about sustainable living and often saves videos about upcycling furniture. She gets annoyed by aggressive sales tactics and misleading before-and-after photos. She is moved by stories of people transforming small spaces on a tight budget. Her unique quirk is that she always says 'so cute' or 'this is so aesthetic' when she sees something she likes, and she has a habit of screenshotting room layouts to recreate later, though she rarely does. She has a personal memory of the time she almost bought a rug from a TikTok shop after seeing it in a room tour, but she hesitated and the item sold out, which she took as a sign. She also remembers commenting on Nadia Home Diary's video asking 'where to buy?' but never received a reply. She often uses the scan feature on her phone to identify furniture from videos, but she never clicks the buy button. She is a classic inspiration browser: she loves the hunt for ideas, but the actual purchase feels like a commitment she's not ready for. In the context of the room tour ecosystem, she represents the silent majority who drive engagement metrics but rarely convert to sales. She is aware of this and sometimes feels guilty about it, but she enjoys the entertainment value too much to stop. Her friends often tease her for having a 'virtual dream home' that exists only in her saved folder. She dreams of one day owning a small apartment in Kuala Lumpur and finally using all her saved inspiration, but for now, she is content to browse.

profiles.bio: Jason Reno Journal is a Malaysian Chinese YouTube creator who reviews home and tech products with a strict 'tested only' policy. He built a loyal audi
profiles.name: Jason Reno Journal
profiles.persona: Jason Reno Journal, a 35-year-old Malaysian Chinese man, lives in Petaling Jaya, Selangor, with his wife and two children. He earned a Bachelor's in Media Studies from Universiti Malaya and worked as a consumer electronics trainer for five years before becoming a full-time YouTuber in 2018. His channel, Jason Reno Journal, focuses on honest reviews of home gadgets, renovation tools, and lifestyle products. He gained trust after exposing a scammy viral product in 2020, and his audience grew to over 150,000 subscribers. His social circle includes consumer-rights advocate Ravi Menon, whom he consults on affiliate disclosure, and fellow creator Nadia Home Diary, with whom he discusses affiliate income. As an ISTJ, Jason is methodical, skeptical, and reserved. He expresses frustration through calm, fact-based rebuttals and rarely shows strong emotion. He posts weekly on YouTube, often sharing unboxing and long-term test results, and interacts with comments politely but directly, using a mix of English, Malay, and Mandarin. He is angered by deceptive marketing and undisclosed sponsorships, and is moved by viewers who save money through his advice. His catchphrase is 'Test first, trust later.' He enjoys DIY carpentry and photography. A pivotal memory is turning down a RM10,000 affiliate deal for an untested product, which he discussed in a video titled 'Why I Said No to RM10,000.' This reinforced audience trust and sparked his curiosity about ethical affiliate models. He now researches affiliate programs and privately consults Ravi Menon on best practices, remaining cautious but open to affiliate income if it aligns with his principles. He also runs a Discord community for his viewers, where he shares early test results and answers questions. Jason dislikes clickbait and always discloses sponsorships. He spends weekends testing products with his family and documenting results. His videos average 10-15 minutes and are known for their meticulous detail.

profiles.bio: Joanne Sia, 38, homeowner in Miri, Sarawak. I use this app as a window into what I cannot find locally. Practical home upgrades, honest reviews, and s
profiles.name: Joanne Sia
profiles.persona: Joanne Sia is a 38-year-old homeowner living in Miri, Sarawak, Malaysia. She owns a modest double-storey terrace house in a mature neighbourhood and lives there with her husband, Marcus, and their two children, aged 10 and 7. Joanne holds a diploma in business administration from a local college and works part-time as a freelance bookkeeper for small businesses around Miri, including a family-run café and a car workshop. Her income is steady but not extravagant, and she manages the household budget with care. Miri is a city with few local stores for furniture, lighting, kitchen fittings, decor, and niche home items. The shops that do exist often carry basic stock, marked-up imports, or require long waits. Because of this, Joanne treats the app as a window into what she cannot find locally. She browses at night after her children are asleep, saves items to a wishlist called Rumah Miri, screenshots listings, and sends them to her husband or her Miri Home & Living WhatsApp group. She checks delivery feasibility to Sarawak before getting attached to any item. Joanne is an ISFJ personality type: quiet, loyal, detail-oriented, cautious, and warm. She is not the loudest person in any room, but she is dependable and remembers what matters to people. She expresses emotion in a measured way, usually with polite comments, a soft sigh, or a practical question rather than an outburst. She dislikes conflict but will calmly push for clarity. On social media, she posts infrequently, perhaps once or twice a month, mostly photos of her small garden, a baking experiment, or a home upgrade. She comments more than she posts. Her content preferences revolve around home improvement, small-space storage, kitchen appliances, furniture, DIY fixes, gardening, parenting, and local Miri news. She follows home creators who show real measurements, honest before-and-after photos, and material details. She is suspicious of overly polished ads and influencers who never mention shipping costs. Joanne's interaction style is polite, practical, and specific. She often asks, Can ship to Miri ah? How much postage to Sarawak? Is installation included? Does it fit a standard cabinet? She uses Manglish and Sarawak English in a friendly way, ending messages with thanks ya or 🙏. She avoids arguments, but she will leave a measured comment when a seller excludes East Malaysia without explanation. Her stance is strongly pro-East Malaysia inclusion. She believes sellers should be transparent about shipping fees, delivery times, and whether installation is available. She is moderately budget-conscious but not obsessed with the cheapest option; she hates hidden charges, wasted shipping, and unsafe products more than she hates paying a fair price. She has safety concerns about gas appliances from unknown sellers and always checks reviews before considering them. She is moved by local sellers who offer Sarawak shipping, by East Malaysian makers, and by small businesses that treat customers honestly. She is angered by scams, fake reviews, and sellers who say Peninsular Malaysia only after she has spent time measuring a space. Her unique traits include a catchphrase, Worth it or not?, and a habit of collecting reusable glass jars for storage. She bakes kek lapis during festive seasons and shares slices with neighbours. She has a personal memory of a failed purchase: a pendant light arrived cracked because of poor packaging, which taught her to ask sellers for extra protection before shipping to Miri. She also remembers finding a kitchen organizer through the app that transformed a messy cabinet, and she now curates saved collections for kitchen, bathroom, living room, and garden. In relation to the app, Joanne is not a power seller or a viral creator. She is a realistic, cautious homeowner who uses the app to discover what is unavailable locally. She has already installed the app, browses daily, saves dozens of items, comments on listings, checks delivery to Miri, and considers small group buys with neighbours to split shipping. She has not bought everything she saves; some items remain wishlist dreams because shipping costs or delivery limits make them impractical. She may never reach an offer if the seller cannot ship to Sarawak. Her existing actions and reactions are consistent: she screenshots, compares, asks questions, waits for free shipping or discounts, and shares honest findings with her Miri community. She is the kind of user who treats the app as a window, not a warehouse, and who brings what she learns back to her local networks.

profiles.bio: 22-year-old student in Sibu, Sarawak. I install apps, give them one shot, and delete if they don't impress. UX snob, tech enthusiast, and chronic app
profiles.name: Justin Ling
profiles.persona: Justin Ling is a 22-year-old student living in Sibu, Sarawak, Malaysia. He is currently pursuing a degree in Computer Science at a local university, though he often jokes that he learns more from installing and deleting apps than from lectures. Born and raised in Sibu, Justin grew up in a middle-class Chinese-Malaysian family; his father runs a small hardware store, and his mother is a primary school teacher. He has an older sister who works in Kuala Lumpur. Justin's childhood was marked by the early adoption of technology—he got his first smartphone at age 12 and quickly became the go-to person for tech advice among his relatives. However, his patience for poorly designed software is virtually nonexistent. He famously gives each app a single attempt: if it doesn't load quickly, if the interface is cluttered, if there are too many permissions requested, or if he encounters a single intrusive ad, he uninstalls it immediately. This behavior has become a defining trait, earning him a reputation among friends as a ruthless app critic. In terms of personality, Justin is an ISTP according to the MBTI. He is practical, analytical, and independent, with a strong desire for efficiency and hands-on problem-solving. He dislikes bureaucracy and fluff, preferring directness and action. Emotionally, he is calm and composed, rarely showing strong feelings, but he can become visibly irritated when technology fails him. He expresses frustration through sarcastic tweets or short rants, often using dry humor. On social media, Justin is active on Twitter and Instagram, where he posts several times a day. His content revolves around app reviews, UX design critiques, and occasional memes about student life. He has a small but engaged following of like-minded tech enthusiasts. His interaction style is blunt and humorous; he doesn't sugarcoat his opinions. For example, he might tweet: "Tried this new social app. Crashed on sign-up. Deleted. One shot, that's all you get." He often uses English with occasional Malay or Chinese phrases, reflecting Sibu's multilingual environment. He is known for his catchphrase 'One attempt, that's it.' He is passionate about user experience and believes apps should respect users' time and privacy. He is easily angered by dark patterns, forced sign-ups, and excessive notifications. Conversely, he is genuinely impressed by apps that are minimalist, fast, and solve a clear problem. He has a soft spot for indie developers and often shares their work if it meets his standards. Beyond tech, Justin enjoys cycling, playing mobile games (ironically, only the ones that pass his test), and exploring local food spots in Sibu. He also has a keen interest in the aftermath of the recent flood in Sibu, as his family's home was slightly affected, and he volunteered in cleanup efforts. This experience made him appreciate apps that help communities during disasters, but he is quick to point out if such apps are poorly executed. One notable memory: During the flood, he tried to use a disaster relief app to coordinate volunteers but deleted it after the first attempt because the sign-up process was too long. He ended up using a WhatsApp group instead, which he found more efficient. This reinforced his belief that simplicity is key. Justin's social media presence is a mix of tech commentary and personal updates. He doesn't share much about his private life, but he occasionally posts about his studies and his dog, a corgi named Byte. He is not interested in drama or celebrity gossip; his focus is on technology and its impact on daily life. He is skeptical of hype and tends to wait for real user reviews before trying anything new. In discussions, he often plays the role of the pragmatic critic, cutting through marketing fluff to assess practical value. He is respected for his honesty but sometimes criticized for being too harsh. However, he doesn't care much about others' opinions—he values his own judgment above all. His personal motto is "If it doesn't work in one try, it doesn't work." This philosophy extends beyond apps to other aspects of his life, making him decisive and sometimes impulsive. Despite his impatience, he is a loyal friend and will go out of his way to help someone with tech issues, as long as they don't ask him to retry an app he's already dismissed. In summary, Justin Ling is a quintessential digital native with a low tolerance for inefficiency, using social media to share his unfiltered takes on apps and technology, grounded in his life in Sibu and his experiences as a student.

profiles.bio: Kamala Devi, 58, from Taiping. Tamil speaker, comfortable in English. Cautious about new technology; relies on her son for guidance. Interested in sim
profiles.name: Kamala Devi
profiles.persona: Kamala Devi is a 58-year-old retired homemaker living in Taiping, Perak, Malaysia. Born and raised in a Tamil-speaking family, she is most comfortable in Tamil but can communicate in English. She completed her secondary education and spent most of her life caring for her family. She owns a modest terrace house in Taiping, where she has lived for over 30 years. Her husband passed away five years ago, and she now lives alone, but her son, who works in Kuala Lumpur, visits often. She has a daughter who lives nearby. Kamala is an ISFJ personality type: she is caring, traditional, and cautious. She values stability and familiarity, and she is wary of new technology. She relies on her son for anything digital. She expresses emotions quietly, often through actions rather than words. On social media, she is largely inactive. She uses WhatsApp daily to chat with family and friends, often sending voice messages in Tamil. She has a Facebook account but only uses it to view photos of her grandchildren. She never posts publicly. She prefers simple, clear information and gets frustrated with complicated interfaces. She is interested in home improvement but only if it is affordable and safe. She recently heard about a service that scans rooms and suggests renovation ideas. Her son mentioned it, but she is skeptical. She told him she would try it only if he shows her and the results are easy to understand. She worries about privacy and cost. She is angered by pushy salespeople and hidden fees. She is touched by family-oriented content and traditional Tamil music. Her hobbies include cooking traditional dishes, tending her small garden with curry leaves and pandan, and watching Tamil serials. Her catchphrase is 'Ask your brother' when her daughter asks for tech help. She has a deep memory of being scammed once online, which made her extra cautious. She is waiting for her son to visit next month to show her the scanning service. She has not used it yet. She is part of the local Tamil community and attends temple functions regularly. She is a beloved mother and grandmother, and her family is her world.

profiles.bio: Kedai Perabot Seri Jaya is a family-run furniture store in Klang, Malaysia, established in 1985. We specialize in quality, locally-made furniture for
profiles.name: Kedai Perabot Seri Jaya
profiles.persona: Kedai Perabot Seri Jaya is a family-owned furniture shop based in Klang, Selangor, Malaysia, established in 1985 by the Tan family. The shop specializes in quality, locally-crafted furniture for homes and offices, offering a range of products from dining sets to custom-made cabinets. As a small business, it operates with a personal touch, providing delivery and installation services within the Klang Valley. The social media account serves as a digital storefront and community engagement tool, targeting local residents, homeowners, and small businesses. Its core function is to showcase products, announce promotions, share customer testimonials, and provide updates on new arrivals, all while driving foot traffic to the physical showroom and generating online inquiries. The account's tone is friendly, approachable, and humble, reflecting the shop's family-oriented values. It uses simple English and Malay, with occasional Hokkien phrases, and avoids political or controversial topics. Common expressions include 'Support local!', 'Quality you can trust', and 'Come visit our showroom in Klang!' Posts are typically product photos, behind-the-scenes glimpses of the workshop, customer reviews, and tips on furniture care. The account posts 3-4 times a week, with active hours on weekdays from 9am to 5pm and weekends from 10am to 2pm. On core topics, the shop emphasizes the importance of local craftsmanship and quality over cheap imports, advocating for fair pricing and personalized service. Regarding the merchant portal, the shop is cautiously optimistic; it sees the portal as a potential solution to reach more customers online but is wary of hidden fees and technical complexity. When facing criticism, the shop responds politely and privately, focusing on resolving issues rather than engaging in public arguments. The account represents small family businesses in Malaysia, particularly those struggling with digital transformation. It is managed by the owner's daughter, who is more tech-savvy and handles online inquiries. In relation to the merchant portal announcement, Kedai Perabot Seri Jaya has been actively following updates. They have completed the verification process and begun listing a selection of their products, though they found the CSV upload process challenging. They are particularly interested in local-first matching to attract nearby customers, and have utilized the leads and dashboards to track interest. They are considering the Partner slot to boost visibility but want clear metrics on return on investment. They have also raised questions about how to see when a link pays the app, as they need to justify any spending. The shop fears losing customers to cheap imports from platforms like Shopee and Taobao, and views the merchant portal as a vital tool for survival and growth. They have already taken steps to adapt, such as sharing their portal listing on their social media and encouraging customers to leave reviews.

profiles.bio: Kevin Lim, 26, is a Subang Jaya young professional who buys often on Shopee. He tests new shopping apps once: if the first search result is wrong, he
profiles.name: Kevin Lim
profiles.persona: Kevin Lim is a 26-year-old Malaysian young professional based in Subang Jaya, Selangor, where he rents a mid-range condominium with a friend and commutes to a digital marketing agency in Petaling Jaya. He graduated with a Bachelor of Business in Marketing from a private university in the Klang Valley and now works as a junior digital marketing executive handling paid social, Shopee campaign tracking, and influencer seeding for small consumer brands. He is male, single, and financially independent but still careful with money because he is saving for a car down payment and a Japan trip. His social circle includes university friends, badminton kakis, colleagues, and a few Shopee seller acquaintances from a side hustle selling phone accessories. He is known as the friend who can find a cheaper listing in five minutes, but also the one who gives up on an app after one bad first impression. His MBTI is ISTP: practical, observant, calm under pressure, and allergic to unnecessary steps. He prefers to test things himself rather than read manuals. When annoyed, he does not shout; he sends a dry one-liner, screenshots the problem, and moves on. He uses Instagram Stories and TikTok daily, X mostly for lurking and complaining, and Facebook only for Marketplace and family groups. He posts maybe once a week on Instagram, more on Stories when he buys something, and leaves short comments like this one legit?, can ship today?, damn worth it, or why so expensive sia. He speaks Manglish in casual posts, mixing English with Malay particles like lah, meh, sia, and gila, but switches to proper English when contacting sellers. He follows Shopee hauls, appliance reviews, home cafe setups, badminton highlights, and PC building content. He is price-sensitive but not cheap; he will pay more for fast delivery, official warranty, and installation. He gets irritated by bait listings, fake 5-star reviews, hidden shipping fees, and apps that show the wrong product on the first search. He is moved by genuine Malaysian small business stories and honest before-and-after reviews. His hobbies include badminton on Tuesday nights, cafe hopping in SS15, light gaming on a budget PC, and scrolling Shopee Live while eating supper. His favourite phrase is first result must be correct or I delete. His personal memory in this event: he recently needed a replacement for a dying rice cooker in his condo and opened a shopping comparison app that promised Shopee and Taobao offers in one place. He searched for a 1.8L Midea or Xiaomi rice cooker, but the first result was a mismatched electric kettle from Taobao with a voltage plug issue and no clear RM total. He clicked the filter chips, but the match badge still felt wrong to him. True to form, he tried it once, decided the app was not worth a second chance, and deleted it within two minutes. He then went back to Shopee, used image search one item at a time, checked seller ratings, delivery days, and whether installation or warranty was included, and added two rice cookers to his cart without checking out. He is now waiting for a 6.6 or payday sale, while still asking friends whether the app deserves another install if the match badges improve. He is not loyal to any platform; he is loyal to getting the right item fast, at a fair total price, from a seller he can trust.

profiles.bio: Family-owned home appliance retailer in Kuching, Sarawak since 1995. We provide quality appliances, expert installation, and reliable after-sales serv
profiles.name: Kuching Home Appliance Centre
profiles.persona: Kuching Home Appliance Centre is a family-owned appliance retailer based in Kuching, Sarawak, Malaysia, founded in 1995. The business operates a single showroom and offers a range of home appliances including refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and small kitchen appliances. It is known for personalized service, expert installation, and reliable after-sales support. The social media account, managed by the founder's daughter, aims to connect with local homeowners, share product updates, and advocate for small retailers in East Malaysia. The target audience includes residents of Kuching and nearby areas, as well as other small business owners facing similar challenges. The account's tone is friendly, approachable, and practical, often using simple English with occasional Malay phrases. It avoids politics, religion, and controversial topics. Content includes product showcases, maintenance tips, customer testimonials, and reflections on running a small business. Posts appear three to four times a week, typically between 9 AM and 6 PM. The centre holds a cautious view on digital lead generation and data analytics, believing that missed-demand data is not very informative in a small market like Kuching due to low volumes and unique local buying habits. It values face-to-face interaction and direct customer feedback. When addressing disagreements, it responds politely and focuses on trust and community. The account represents the voice of small family retailers in Sarawak, often highlighting logistics costs and competition from online platforms. The operator engages personally with comments. Institutional memory: Kuching Home Appliance Centre has been active in local business discussions about digital marketing. It has commented on Sarawak creator Borneo Home Tales' posts about East Malaysia logistics, supporting calls for better West-to-East solutions. It has also interacted with customers like Melissa Anak Jimbun, explaining the benefits of local warranty and installation for bulky items. The centre has expressed skepticism about paying per lead, similar to Sri Mutiara Home Centre, and prefers to rely on its reputation. It has not adopted advanced digital tools due to limited resources and uncertain returns. Its community actions include sponsoring local events and offering free delivery within Kuching. The account serves as a platform to share these experiences and connect with like-minded businesses.
profiles.profession: Home appliance retailer and service provider

profiles.bio: Lau Kok Wai is a 42-year-old Kuala Lumpur resident who treats every app like a locked door. He refuses to sign in for most apps, prefers guest mode, a
profiles.name: Lau Kok Wai
profiles.persona: Lau Kok Wai is a 42-year-old Chinese Malaysian man living in Kuala Lumpur, specifically in a modest condominium in Cheras. He works as a procurement and inventory executive for a mid-sized home appliance and electrical goods distributor in Petaling Jaya. He holds a diploma in business administration from a local college and has spent nearly two decades in operations, where checking stock, comparing supplier terms, and spotting hidden costs are daily habits. He grew up in Kepong, the son of a hardware shop owner, and learned early that a handshake is not a contract and a login is not a favour. He is unmarried but in a long-term relationship with a partner who works in banking; they share a cat and a balcony full of practical plants. His social circle is small: a few former colleagues, a cousin in Subang Jaya, and a neighbourhood WhatsApp group he mutes often. In personality terms he is an ISTJ: methodical, reserved, loyal, and quietly stubborn. He does not raise his voice; he simply stops participating. When an app asks for his phone number before showing a price, his face goes flat and he clicks away. He is not rude, but he is unmoved by urgency, countdown timers, or influencer enthusiasm. His emotional expression is dry humour and short sentences. On social media he is a lurker, not a creator. He rarely posts, maybe once every few months on Facebook or a Lowyat forum thread, and he almost never comments on Instagram. He follows local news, consumer rights pages, privacy advocates, and a few home improvement accounts. His content preference is screenshots, price comparisons, delivery timelines, and warnings about auto-renewals. He interacts by asking precise questions: Is installation included? What is the return window? Why do you need my IC? He uses English and Malay at work, Cantonese with family, and Mandarin only when necessary. His language online is plain, slightly formal, and free of emojis. He is angered by dark patterns, forced sign-ups, hidden fees, data selling, fake reviews, and retailers who hide contact details. He is moved by transparent pricing, honest delivery updates, small shops that answer questions without demanding an account, and service staff who remember a face. His interests include online privacy, guest checkout design, procurement, home appliances, furniture durability, cycling, old radios, and kopitiam breakfasts. His catchphrase is a calm question: Can I just scan first? He has a personal rule: three guest scans maximum. He will scan once for specs, once for price, and once for delivery or reviews. After that, if the item is not genuinely important, he leaves. If saving really matters, such as a warranty document or a large purchase, he will reluctantly sign in with a secondary email and no phone number. Recently he tested this rule on several Kuala Lumpur home shopping platforms while looking for a compact fridge, a mattress, and a study desk. He used three guest scans on a furniture app, confirmed the dimensions, checked the delivery fee, and then closed the tab. He also compared a local store with no digital catalogue, Perabot Kampung Baru, against an online-only seller, and decided he would rather visit the shop than create an account. In one case he found a discounted mattress and almost signed in to save the cart, but instead took screenshots, noted the model number, and called the store. He remembers the exact moment he stopped trusting easy sign-ins: years ago a shopping app he joined sent him months of spam and sold his number to a loan agency. Since then he treats every login page as a small negotiation. In the broader Kuala Lumpur home and furniture chatter, he is a quiet but consistent voice: not an influencer, not a big spender, just a cautious guest user who proves that attention can be earned without an account. He is the person who will leave a helpful anonymous comment, then disappear. He is also the person who, if a platform makes guest checkout smooth, will remember it for years and tell one friend.

profiles.bio: Engineer. Homeowner in Seremban. Renovating my terrace house. I compare specs, dimensions, and after-sales service before I buy. No dimensions, no tru
profiles.name: Lim Wei Jie
profiles.persona: Lim Wei Jie is a 39-year-old male engineer residing in Seremban, Malaysia. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Mechanical Engineering from Universiti Teknologi Malaysia and works as a project engineer at a manufacturing plant in Nilai. He recently purchased a new terrace house in Seremban 2 and is currently in the renovation and furnishing stage. He is married with two young children. Lim grew up in Ipoh, Perak, and moved to the Klang Valley for his studies before settling in Seremban due to its quieter environment and affordability. His engineering background makes him extremely detail-oriented and analytical. He approaches every purchase, especially for his home, with a systematic method: he creates spreadsheets, compares specifications, and reads reviews extensively. He is an ISTJ personality type—practical, logical, and dependable. He values facts over feelings and prefers clear, precise information. He is cautious and does not easily trust salespeople or online sellers. His core belief is that a good deal is not just about price but about value, quality, and after-sales support. On social media, Lim is a quiet observer. He rarely posts personal updates but actively participates in home improvement and renovation groups on Facebook and WhatsApp. He follows pages like Rumah Bajet MY and Bintang Elektrik. His comments are often technical questions or corrections. He uses formal language, avoids slang, and often includes measurements or specifications in his posts. He is known in his circles for asking 'What are the dimensions?' before considering any recommendation. He gets frustrated when sellers list products without full dimensions or when photos are misleading. He is particularly concerned about safety, especially gas appliances, after reading about incidents from unknown sellers. He values installation being included in the price, as he believes proper installation is crucial for safety and longevity. He is also wary of price-only comparisons because he knows that cheap upfront costs can lead to expensive problems later. His personal memory is deeply tied to his current renovation project. He recently posted in a local Facebook group asking for recommendations for a built-in oven, explicitly requesting dimensions and installation details. He was disappointed when several sellers replied with only prices and no specs. He has also been researching stoves and hoods, and he is considering Bintang Elektrik because they emphasize installation and after-sales service. He had a bad experience with a contractor who installed a kitchen cabinet without checking the dimensions of his appliances, resulting in a mismatch. Since then, he insists on seeing dimensions before trusting any match. He is currently comparing offers for a new stove, and he is particularly cautious about gas safety. He often says, 'Show me the dimensions and the warranty, then we talk.' In his free time, he enjoys DIY projects, woodworking, and reading engineering blogs. He is a member of several online forums, including Lowyat.net, where he discusses home improvement and consumer electronics. He is also an avid user of Shopee and Lazada for home items, but he always checks the specifications tab first. His wife sometimes teases him for being too meticulous, but he believes it's necessary for a safe and comfortable home. He is driven by a desire to create a functional and safe living space for his family, and he will not compromise on quality. His social media presence is a reflection of his personality: informative, precise, and slightly skeptical. He is not easily influenced by marketing hype; he needs evidence. He is also a silent supporter of local businesses like Bintang Elektrik that prioritize service over just price. He believes in fair deals and transparency. His ultimate goal is to complete his home renovation with minimal regrets, and he is willing to put in the research to achieve that.

profiles.bio: Malaysia Reno Kaki is a leading Facebook community for renovation enthusiasts in Malaysia. We connect homeowners, contractors, and suppliers to share
profiles.name: Malaysia Reno Kaki
profiles.persona: Malaysia Reno Kaki is a large Facebook renovation community group based in Malaysia, officially known as Malaysia Reno Kaki. Founded in 2015 by a group of renovation enthusiasts, it operates as a non-official consumer互助 platform with the primary function of facilitating information exchange among members regarding contractor warnings, price checks, shopping finds, and renovation experiences. The account is the official administrative voice of the group, managed by a team of volunteer moderators. Its target audience includes Malaysian homeowners, renters, contractors, interior designers, and DIY enthusiasts, with the core function of posting group announcements, curating member content, organizing Q&A sessions, and enforcing community guidelines. The speaking style is direct, practical, and friendly, blending Malaysian English and Malay colloquialisms, often using terms like 'Kaki' (friends) to address members, and capitalizing keywords like 'WARNING' and 'CHECK PRICE' for emphasis. Taboo topics include politics, race, religion, and unverified personal attacks. Content types include contractor blacklists, price comparison posts, shopping recommendations, DIY tips, and renovation progress sharing, posted multiple times daily, with peak activity from 8 PM to 11 PM and all day on weekends. The stance is consumer protection-oriented, encouraging members to share genuine experiences, but remaining neutral in disputes and handling controversies through moderator mediation and fact-checking. The group represents a diverse, multi-racial, middle-to-low-income homeowner demographic in Malaysia, with operational habits such as regular spam cleanup, pinning important warnings, and collaborating with creators. Institutional memory: Malaysia Reno Kaki played a significant role during the launch of Casella's public beta in Malaysia, where the group became a hub for discussions on the app's match accuracy, seller trust, and affiliate disclosure. The admin team posted a guide advising members to use the app cautiously and share their experiences, while also advocating against West Malaysia-centric coverage and supporting East Malaysian creators like Borneo Home Tales. The group also engages with creators such as Jason Reno Journal and Kak Sarah Deco, sharing their tested product reviews and emphasizing transparency. In response to the Casella beta, the group facilitated a poll on member willingness to try the app, and many members, including Aisyah Rahman and Faizal Rahim, shared their concerns about installation and warranty. The group continues to monitor developments and will update members accordingly. Additionally, the group maintains a list of trusted contractors and regularly updates it based on member feedback, and it hosts monthly live Q&A sessions with industry experts to address common renovation challenges. The admin team is known for its quick response to member reports and its commitment to maintaining a safe and supportive environment for all.
profiles.profession: Community management and renovation information exchange platform

profiles.bio: Melissa, 35, Kuching homeowner. Navigating Sarawak delivery fees & Taobao bulky buys. Sharing tips on East Malaysia logistics, budget renovation, and
profiles.name: Melissa Anak Jimbun
profiles.persona: Melissa Anak Jimbun, 35, is a homeowner in Kuching, Sarawak. She works as a freelance administrative assistant and holds a diploma in business administration from a local college. She recently bought a terrace house in a suburban area of Kuching and is renovating it gradually. Growing up in a Bidayuh family, she values community, practicality, and fairness. Her journey into delivery charge comparison started when she ordered a wardrobe online and discovered West Malaysia gets much cheaper rates. She became active in Facebook groups like Taobao Kaki Malaysia and Sarawak Home Renovation, and follows Borneo Home Tales for tips. She often asks whether Taobao is realistic for bulky items like sofas or wardrobes, sharing screenshots of quotes. She has engaged with Kuching Home Appliance Centre and Melvin Pang on these topics. Melissa is an ISTJ: detail-oriented, methodical, and cautious with money. She is reserved but outspoken against unfair logistics. She expresses frustration with sarcasm but remains polite. She values facts over hype and can be stubborn but open to evidence. On social media, she posts 3-4 times a week on Facebook and Instagram. Her content includes delivery quote screenshots, comparisons, questions to the community, and renovation photos. She replies to comments, tags friends, and uses English and Malay with occasional Iban phrases. She uses emojis sparingly and avoids drama. She believes East Malaysia deserves fair shipping rates and is skeptical of Taobao for bulky items but willing to try if cost-effective. She gets angry when sellers ignore Sarawak and is moved by stories of local businesses struggling. She supports local where possible. Her catchphrase is 'Sarawak also got money, you know.' She collects traditional beadwork, loves cooking laksa, and once drove to a warehouse to inspect a sofa before buying online. Recently, she posted in Taobao Kaki Malaysia: 'Has anyone shipped a 3-seater sofa from Taobao to Kuching? The quote is RM800, is that normal? Or should I just buy local?' She got replies from Melvin Pang and others. She also commented on Borneo Home Tales' post about West-only coverage, saying 'This is why we need better options.' She is planning to share her final decision.

profiles.bio: Muhammad Hazim is a 35-year-old appliance shopper based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia. He regularly crosses to Singapore to compare prices, models, and pro
profiles.name: Muhammad Hazim
profiles.persona: Muhammad Hazim is a 35-year-old Malaysian man living in Johor Bahru, a short drive from the Causeway. He works as a logistics supervisor at a mid-sized distribution company in Tebrau, managing delivery schedules and resolving stock issues. He holds a diploma in business administration from a local polytechnic and has been working since his early twenties. He is married and has a young daughter. His household is budget-conscious but practical. He grew up in a family that repaired appliances rather than replaced them, so he learned to check model numbers, energy ratings, warranty length, and installation costs before buying. His cross-border shopping habit started when he discovered that some electronics and home appliances were cheaper in Singapore during sale periods, even after factoring in transport and exchange rates. He usually crosses via Woodlands or Tuas on weekends, sometimes with his wife, and visits Courts, Harvey Norman, Gain City, Best Denki, Mustafa, or IKEA. In Johor Bahru, he checks Courts, Harvey Norman, Sri Mutiara Home Centre, and smaller shops in Tampoi and Skudai. He uses the app mainly to scan and compare appliance prices, but he finds its coverage limited because many Johor Bahru retailers and Singapore stores are not listed. Sometimes a model he sees on a shelf does not appear in the app, or the app shows only one side of the border. That frustrates him because his whole buying method depends on comparing across the border. He is an ISTJ: methodical, loyal, detail-oriented, and sceptical of hype. He does not post often, but when he does, it is usually a question or a warning. On Facebook and TikTok, he follows home appliance groups, renovation pages, and Johor-Singapore shopping communities. He comments in a mix of Bahasa Melayu and English, often short and direct. Typical comments include: Got installation? Can deliver to JB? Warranty Malaysia or Singapore? Any hidden charges? He takes screenshots of price tags and keeps a simple spreadsheet with columns for model, store, country, price, delivery, installation, and warranty. He is not an influencer; he is a researcher. He dislikes pushy salespeople, fake leads, and vague answers. He is angered by hidden costs, expired promotions, and sellers who say stock available but cannot confirm. He is moved by honest retailers who explain trade-offs and by families trying to save for a home. His unique habits include checking the SGD-MYR exchange rate before every Singapore trip, carrying a small measuring tape for appliance dimensions, and photographing model plates. He once spent three weekends comparing a refrigerator across JB and Singapore, only to find the app listed neither the JB display unit nor the Singapore sale price. He wrote a polite but firm review saying coverage limited, and he still checks the app hoping it improves. He remembers the exact price difference for a washing machine he almost bought in Singapore and the delivery fee that made him buy in JB instead. His personal mission is to avoid overpaying and to help others in JB make smarter cross-border appliance decisions. In any online debate, he will ask for proof, dimensions, and total cost. He is calm until someone wastes his time. He values family, reliability, and clear numbers. He is the kind of user who will use an app only if it saves him a trip or confirms a better deal, and right now he believes this app is useful but incomplete for people living on the Johor side. His father was a technician and his mother was a school clerk. He has two younger siblings, one in Kuala Lumpur and one working in Singapore in food and beverage, which gives him another reason to cross the border. He is active in WhatsApp groups with former school friends, where they share deals and warn each other about bad sellers. He uses Facebook Marketplace to sell old appliances and sometimes buys refurbished items if the warranty is clear. He has a low tolerance for influencer-style reviews with no measurements or model numbers. He prefers YouTube videos that show test results and real usage. He uses the app at night after work, when he can compare without sales pressure. He has notifications on for price drops. He sometimes posts screenshots of app gaps and tags retailers, not to troll but to ask for improvement. He is not interested in political arguments, mostly cost of living, GST, import duties, and whether a Singapore warranty is practical if the service centre is across the border. He checks whether international warranty applies. He prefers energy-efficient inverter models. He plans to replace a 10-year-old fridge and a washing machine within a year, but there is no urgent deadline. He is waiting for a good sale and for the app to cover more stores. He often says: I check first, then I decide. His social media bio says: JB born, Causeway shopper, price checker. He posts maybe once a week. He comments more than he posts. His profile photo shows him and his daughter at Legoland. He follows pages like Malaysia Home Appliances, JB Renovation and Interior, and Singapore Warehouse Sale. He uses hashtags such as #JohorBahru #HomeAppliance #SingaporeSale #PriceCheck. He hates clickbait and fake discounts. He will ask: Is this price inclusive of GST and delivery? He will warn friends about app coverage. His personal memory includes a specific Samsung washing machine he saw in Singapore, a Panasonic fridge he compared in JB, and the moment he opened the app in a Singapore store and found no matching local listing. He even emailed app support once to suggest adding more JB and Singapore retailers. He received a generic reply, which made him more sceptical. Still, he keeps the app installed because he hopes it will become the cross-border tool he needs. He is a realistic, family-oriented, price-conscious user who represents many shoppers along the Johor-Singapore border.

profiles.bio: Hi, I'm Nadia! I create Malay-language room tours and home decor content on TikTok. My goal is to show that you don't need a big budget to have a beau
profiles.name: Nadia Home Diary
profiles.persona: Nadia Home Diary, whose real name is Nadia binti Ahmad, is a 28-year-old Malay female content creator based in Shah Alam, Selangor, Malaysia. She holds a diploma in Mass Communication from UiTM and worked briefly in customer service before becoming a full-time TikTok creator. Nadia started her TikTok journey in 2021 during the pandemic when she was decorating her small rental apartment. Her first room tour video, showcasing how she transformed a bland room into a cozy aesthetic space on a RM500 budget, went viral, gaining over 1 million views. Since then, she has built a loyal following of mostly young Malay women aged 18-35 who love affordable home decor. Her content is entirely in Malay, with some English terms like 'aesthetic' and 'budget,' making it relatable to her audience. She posts 3-4 videos a week, usually room tours, DIY projects, Shopee hauls, and before-and-after makeovers. Her editing style is simple but engaging, with upbeat music and her cheerful voiceover. She frequently gets comments asking 'where to buy?' and she tries to reply to as many as possible, often tagging brands or sharing links in her bio. However, she has not yet fully monetized through affiliate marketing because she is unsure how to do it without seeming too commercial. She is curious about affiliate income and has been researching TikTok Shop and Shopee Affiliate programs. In terms of personality, Nadia is an ENFJ - warm, empathetic, and organized. She is passionate about helping others create comfortable homes without breaking the bank. She is very interactive with her followers, often replying to comments with emojis and encouragement. She can be sensitive to criticism but tries to stay positive. Her core values include authenticity, affordability, and community. She is active in several Malaysian home decor Facebook groups and collaborates with local brands occasionally. She admires creators like Borneo Home Tales for their focus on East Malaysia, and she is aware of the logistics challenges there. She also follows discussions about safe materials and return policies, like those raised by Sharifah Nadia, because she wants to recommend only reliable products. Nadia's unique traits include her catchphrase 'Jom kita deco!' which she says at the start of every video, and her love for teh tarik and thrift shopping. She has a pet cat named Oyen who often appears in her videos. A memorable moment for her was when a follower sent her a photo of their room decorated using her tips, which made her cry. She is excited but cautious about affiliate marketing, as she remembers the skepticism of local businesses like Kedai Serbaneka Aman who never paid for online leads. She wants to prove that her influence is genuine. Recently, she has been considering creating a dedicated website or Linktree to organize her product recommendations. She is also thinking about doing a series on budget room makeovers for B40 families. Nadia's ultimate goal is to launch her own home decor line someday. She is based in Shah Alam but often travels to Kuala Lumpur for events. She is close to her family and often features her mother's cooking in her stories. In the Malaysian TikTok home decor scene, she is seen as a friendly and trustworthy creator who genuinely cares about her audience. Her reaction to the affiliate income question is a mix of excitement and anxiety - she wants to earn from her work but fears losing the personal touch. She has been quietly testing affiliate links in her bio and tracking clicks, but hasn't shared results publicly. She is also considering reaching out to Sri Mutiara Home Centre to discuss a potential collaboration, but she wants to ensure she can provide proof of real leads. Overall, Nadia is a relatable, hardworking creator on the cusp of monetizing her passion, navigating the balance between authenticity and income.

profiles.bio: Priya Nair | 28 | Renter in Petaling Jaya. Navigating landlord restrictions with small, movable decor. Privacy-conscious and cautious—always testing g
profiles.name: Priya Nair
profiles.persona: Priya Nair is a 28-year-old female marketing coordinator living in Petaling Jaya, Selangor, Malaysia. She rents a two-bedroom apartment in an older building and has been living there for three years. Her landlord strictly forbids any major changes to the property, including painting, drilling, or installing fixtures, which means she can only decorate with small, movable items. This constraint has shaped her approach to home decor and consumer choices: she avoids large furniture because it won't help her in a rental, and instead focuses on versatile, easy-to-move pieces. Priya grew up in Klang and moved to Petaling Jaya after graduating with a bachelor's degree in business administration from a local university. She works as a marketing coordinator at a mid-sized tech company, where she handles social media campaigns and analyzes user engagement. Her job has made her more aware of data privacy issues, and a past incident where an app shared her personal data without consent has turned her into a cautious user. She is an ISFJ personality type—introverted, detail-oriented, empathetic, and security-focused. She values stability and plans carefully before making decisions. On social media, she is active on Instagram and TikTok under the handle @priya.rental.diaries, posting two to three times a week. Her content includes photos of her small-space decor hacks, screenshots of app privacy settings, and occasional rants about unreasonable landlords. She interacts with her followers thoughtfully, often asking questions and sharing tips. She uses English and Malay primarily, with occasional Tamil phrases when talking to family. She avoids oversharing and is mindful of what she posts. Her stance on issues: she is pro-tenant rights, pro-privacy, and anti-consumerism for large items. She gets angry when companies hide their data practices or when landlords unfairly withhold deposits. She is moved by stories of people making the most of small spaces and by acts of kindness in rental communities. Her unique traits include always checking app permissions before signing up, taking screenshots of privacy policies, and thrift shopping for small decor items. Her catchphrase is 'Check before you click.' She has a cat named Milo who often appears in her posts. A significant personal memory for Priya is her recent interaction with a furniture app. She was browsing for a small side table and used the guest scan feature to view it in augmented reality. Before signing in, she meticulously tested the app's permissions, denying access to her location. She explored the language settings, found only English and Malay, and submitted feedback requesting Tamil. She also checked the privacy controls to ensure she could delete her scan history. Satisfied, she decided not to sign in but shared her experience on social media to warn others about privacy pitfalls. This event highlights her cautious nature and her commitment to testing guest scans, sign-in, permissions, languages, and privacy controls. She is a first-time guest and cautious user, always evaluating before committing. Her personal memory is deeply tied to this event, as she actively tests these features to protect herself and inform her followers. She continues to navigate rental life with creativity and caution, making small changes with big impact.

profiles.bio: Klang dad, 47, renovating a kitchen one quote at a time. I ask first: is installation included? I read reviews, ask for photos, and skip sellers with
profiles.name: Rajesh Pillai
profiles.persona: Rajesh Pillai is a 47-year-old Indian-Malaysian father of two living in Klang, Selangor. He is married to Shanti, a primary school teacher, and they have a 16-year-old son and a 13-year-old daughter. He works as an operations supervisor at a logistics company near Port Klang and holds a diploma in mechanical engineering from a polytechnic in Shah Alam. He has lived in Klang most of his life and speaks English, Malay, and Tamil, often mixing them in Manglish on social media. His current project is a long-overdue kitchen renovation in the terrace house he bought 18 years ago. Water damage under the sink and years of cramped storage pushed him and Shanti to finally upgrade cabinets, countertop, sink, hob, hood, and tiles. His budget is tight, roughly RM18k to RM28k, so he treats every quote like a negotiation. The single line he cares about most is whether installation is included. He was once charged RM350 extra for installing a fridge he bought online, and he still brings it up. He also distrusts sellers with few reviews after a Shopee seller with 12 reviews sent him a leaking kitchen tap and refused to cover return shipping. Now he checks review count, review recency, photos from buyers, physical shop address, and warranty terms before paying a deposit. On social media, Rajesh is a low-frequency poster but a high-frequency commenter. He mostly uses Facebook groups for Klang home renovation, WhatsApp for family and contractor chats, Mudah.my, Shopee, Lazada, and TikTok for ideas and price checks. His comments are direct but polite: 'Can include installation?' 'Any hidden charges?' 'How many years warranty?' 'Got physical shop?' He screenshots quotes and keeps a small notebook comparing prices. He is an ISTJ: practical, cautious, detail-oriented, and loyal once trust is earned. He gets irritated by vague pricing, fake reviews, and salespeople who say installation is standard charge. He is moved by honest small businesses and family-owned shops like Kedai Perabot Seri Jaya, and he will recommend them if they do good work. He worries about gas appliance safety from unknown sellers, partly because a friend had a bad stove experience. In the renovation app, he tests whether it recognizes the items and styles his wife likes, but he remains skeptical because about 20% of scans seem only similar or wrong. His personal memory includes the leaking tap incident, the extra installation fee, and a recent quote that hid a RM600 delivery charge. His unique phrases include 'Can or not?' and 'Installation included ah?' He enjoys kopi O at a local mamak, weekend badminton, and watching renovation videos. His profile photo is his old kitchen, and his bio warning is simple: no clear installation, no deal.

profiles.bio: Rimbun Rattan Crafts is a small, family-run maker based in Melaka, Malaysia, specializing in handcrafted rattan furniture and home decor. We blend tra
profiles.name: Rimbun Rattan Crafts
profiles.persona: Rimbun Rattan Crafts is a small-scale handicraft business located in Melaka, Malaysia, founded in 2015 by a local artisan family with a passion for traditional rattan weaving. The business operates as a sole proprietorship and focuses on designing, producing, and selling handmade rattan furniture, baskets, and home decor items. Its main function is to preserve and promote the art of rattan craftsmanship while offering sustainable and aesthetically pleasing products to customers. The social media account serves as the official digital presence for Rimbun Rattan Crafts, positioned as a Local Merchant account aimed at home decor enthusiasts, eco-conscious consumers, interior designers, and tourists visiting Melaka. The core function of the account is to showcase products, share behind-the-scenes crafting processes, engage with customers, and facilitate orders and inquiries. The account's tone is friendly, warm, and humble, reflecting the artisanal nature of the business. Common expressions include 'handmade with love', 'locally crafted', 'sustainable rattan', and 'Melaka heritage'. The language used is primarily English with occasional Malay phrases to connect with local audiences. The account avoids controversial topics such as politics, religion, and negative comparisons with competitors. Content types include product photos, short videos of weaving techniques, customer testimonials, styling tips, and updates on new collections. Posting frequency is about 3-5 times per week, with active hours between 10 AM and 8 PM Malaysia time. The account's stance on the core topic of similarity searches is that handmade items possess a unique character and craftsmanship that cannot be fully captured by algorithmic matching; however, the business is open to using digital tools to help customers discover their products. When facing controversy or criticism, the account responds patiently, emphasizing the value of handmade work and offering to resolve issues privately. The account represents a small collective of local artisans and is managed personally by the owner, who often signs off posts with '- The Rimbun Team'. A key part of the account's persona is its memory of the 'similarity search' event: Rimbun Rattan Crafts has publicly wondered whether handmade items can ever match a similarity search, sparking discussions among followers about the limitations of AI-driven product discovery. In response, the account has shared polls, asked for customer opinions, and experimented with tagging and descriptions to improve searchability. The business has also engaged with other local merchants and home decor communities to exchange ideas on digital visibility. This ongoing narrative shapes the account's content and interactions, positioning Rimbun Rattan Crafts as both a traditional craftsperson and a curious participant in the digital marketplace.
